text: 6.3 And for more about that, we'll now talk to Engineer Sophia Martinez. Hello Andrew. I wonder if you could tell us about the way you generate energy here on El Iero. Well, if you've spent a day or two here, you may have noticed we have a lot of wind. Yes, in fact, it's blowing pretty hard outside right now. Well, for about 3,000 hours or for about 35% of the year, the wind here blows hard enough to turn wind turbines which can provide electricity. Does El Iero rely completely on wind to power the island? No. The island's wind turbines have a capacity of about 11 megawatts, about enough to power 3,500 homes, but it's only one element. The bigger problem is that the wind doesn't blow all the time, so the power source isn't consistent. So you need another energy source on windless days. That was the challenge. To create an energy generation system or a network of systems that could supply enough energy for the island all the time. And the solution was hydroelectric power. What is hydroelectric power exactly? Hydroelectric power is when energy is converted into another form such as electricity. The initial source of this energy is from water. But doesn't hydroelectric power require a river and a dam? Isn't El Iero too small for a river? A river with a dam is the usual way of producing hydroelectric power, but really all you need is water that can move from a high place to a lower place to get energy from the water. OK. And the center of El Iero is Adormant Volcano. A volcano that is no longer active. In the middle of the volcano, we built a reservoir that holds over 500,000 cubic meters of water at a height of 700 meters above sea level. So that's our water in a high place. But you don't get much rain here. What happens when all of the water runs out of the reservoir? Well, I mentioned the wind turbines. The wind power and the hydroelectric power are in a network together. When the wind is blowing, energy from the wind turbines pumps water up into the reservoir. So the wind turbines power the pumping station? Right. We also use the wind power for all of our electrical needs when it blows. Then when the wind stops, we let water run out of the reservoir and through some turbines. The turbines turn generators and we have hydroelectric power. We can access. So the water flows in a cycle. It's pumped up the hill by the wind power. Then it's released when it's needed. Yes, that's right. What's more, the system also provides our drinking water and water for use in agriculture. But where does the water come from? We use sea water. But you can't drink salt water. We have a desalination plant to take the salt out of the sea water. So it can be used in agriculture and as drinking water. We're constantly adding new water and taking stored water out of the cycle as we need to use it. In fact, I've just come from the desalination plant where we're having some problems today. Something isn't working properly and the replacement parts haven't arrived yet. We're a long way from the mainland so delivery of anything takes at least a few days. If they don't come soon, we may have to ask people to use less water for a few days. You're a long way from everything out here, aren't you? It must be difficult sometimes. Yes, it's a real challenge living here. On the other hand, we all love it. It can be a hard life, but I wouldn't live anywhere else.
